question:
A 71-year-old male nursing home resident with a history of vascular dementia, type 2 diabetes,
coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, frequent falls, and stage 3A chronic kidney disease presents
for a follow-up visit. He requires assistance with daily activities such as bathing, dressing, and toileting.
Since his last visit six months ago, he has experienced one fall. His current medications include
metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, rosuvastatin 5 mg daily, and apixaban 5 mg twice
daily. On examination, his blood pressure is 113/84 mm Hg, heart rate is 89 beats per minute, and
temperature is normal. He weighs 64.5 kg, reflecting a 4-kg weight loss since his previous visit. Cardiac
examination reveals an irregularly irregular rhythm. His score on the Clinical Frailty Scale is 6,
indicating moderate frailty. Laboratory results show a glycated hemoglobin level of 8.2% (reference
range, 4.3–5.6), a serum creatinine level of 1.4 mg/dL (0.8–1.3), and an estimated glomerular filtration
rate of 52 mL/min/1.73 m² (≥60). Six months earlier, his glycated hemoglobin level was 7.6%, and his
serum creatinine level was 1.4 mg/dL. All other laboratory findings are unremarkable. What is the most
appropriate next step in managing this patient’s diabetes? Answer Choices: (A) Add glimepiride (B)
Add pioglitazone (C) Start GLP-1 receptor agonist (D) Continue the current regimen (E) Add
empagliflozin (F) Switch to insulin therapy (G) Add insulin (H) Increase metformin dose to 1500 mg
twice daily (I) Switch to sulfonylurea monotherapy (J) Add sitagliptin
 A. Switch to insulin therapy
B. Add glimepiride
C. Continue the current regimen
D. Add insulin
E. Switch to sulfonylurea monotherapy
F. Add sitagliptin
G. Add pioglitazone
H. Add empagliflozin
I. Start GLP-1 receptor agonist
J. Increase metformin dose to 1500 mg twice daily
